caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:001641
attempts.paper_title: Validation of Decision-Making Models and Analysis of Decision Variables in the Rat Basal Ganglia
attempts.entry_title: Decision-making models and decision variables in the rat ventral basal ganglia (Ito and Doya 2009)
attempts.summary: Most behavioral findings held: choices depend on reward history, with switching after non-reward. The advantage of time-varying F-Q and DF-Q models held in part (0.5374 and 0.5369 against the paper's 0.5375 and 0.5368). The tests comparing the models could not be settled, because the Q update equation and the training and test split are missing from the paper. In NAc and VP, state, action and reward coding reproduced, and the ventral pallidum's larger share of action value neurons held only in part. Reward information was above threshold before the poke, which the test criterion did not allow. The core versus shell comparison could not be tested, because the dataset does not label them.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Ito and Doya (2009) on dandiset 001641, which holds the behaviour of six rats in 70 sessions of a probabilistic free-choice task and 214 single units from the nucleus accumbens and ventral pallidum. It covers the trial counts and choice history (Fig. 2), the least-squares and maximum-likelihood fits of Markov and Q-learning models with constant and time-varying parameters (Fig. 3 to 5, Tables 1 to 3), and the coding of state, action, reward and action values by the neurons (Fig. 8 and 9).

notebooks.title: Reproducing Ito and Doya (2009) from dandiset 001641

outcomes.statement: The analysis covers 60,221 trials in 70 recording sessions from six rats, of which 39,175 are choice trials, 12,707 no-choice trials and 8329 error trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral data, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Here, we report the results of all 60,221 trials in 70 recording sessions performed by six rats, consisting of 39,175 choice trials (65.1%), 12,707 no-choice trials (21.1%), and 8329 error trials (13.8%)
outcomes.notes: Both readings of the total give 60,211 trials, as every trial has a cue tone. Choice, no-choice and error trials are 39,175, 12,707 and 8329, exactly as reported, in 70 sessions from 6 rats. The paper's own parts sum to 60,211, 10 fewer than its stated total of 60,221.
deviations: Choice trials are tone-A trials with result 1 or 3 and an L or R choice, no-choice trials tone-B trials with result 1, and all others errors; the result codes are not described in the files and were read from the other columns.

outcomes.statement: A block took 105.6 trials on average, and a session held 8.1 blocks on average, from 5 to 12.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral data, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: On average, 105.6 trials were required in one block, and 8.1 blocks (from 5 to 12 blocks) were performed in one session
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), all trials and every block, 104.9 trials per block and 8.2 blocks per session, 5 to 12. Counting completed blocks only gives 7.44 blocks and a fewest of 4; counting choice trials only gives 68 to 70 trials per block. Blocks are those of the BlockDesign table (574, of which 521 finished).

outcomes.statement: In choice trials the time from center-hole exit to L or R hole entry was under 1 s in 72% of trials, with a median of 0.75 s.
outcomes.source: Results, Reaction time and tone discrimination, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: The reaction time in the choice trials, the time period from the exit of the center hole to the entry of the left or right hole, was <1 s in 72% of the trials and had a median of 0.75 s
outcomes.notes: 72.1% of choice-trial reaction times are under 1 s, median 0.754 s, over 39,172 trials. Three choice trials have a negative reaction time (L or R entry recorded before the center exit) and are left out; keeping them changes neither value. The rats range from 35.0% to 91.3% under 1 s.
deviations: Three trials with a negative reaction time were left out as timing errors.

outcomes.statement: Rats rarely failed to poke after tone A (0.39% of choice trials) or poked wrongly after tone B (0.73% of no-choice trials), so they discriminated the tones well.
outcomes.source: Results, Reaction time and tone discrimination, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: The errors in the choice trials, in which rats did not perform any nose pokes within 1 min for tone A presentation, were only 0.39% of the choice trials. The errors in no-choice trials, in which rats performed a nose poke at the left or right hole within 1 s for tone B presentation, were 0.73% of the no-choice trials
outcomes.notes: Counted from the event series, 317 tone-A trials in which the rat held the cue and made no L or R entry within 60 s (0.81% of choice trials, 0.80% with the errors in the denominator) and 129 tone-B trials with an L or R entry within 1 s of center exit (1.02% and 1.01%). 96 of the 317 tone-A trials had a cue tone under 1 s (1st percentile 0.12 s), shorter than any cue of the task (1000 to 2000 ms), so the tone probably stopped when the rat left early and the hold test let these through; keeping tones of at least 1 s gives 221 and 125 trials (0.56% and 0.98%). Counted from the rare result codes 5 (tone A) and 4 (tone B), whose tones last over 1 s (1st percentile 1.05 and 1.03 s), 0.27% and 1.11%. No numerator gives both of the paper's 0.39% and 0.73% under either denominator. The outcome rests on the tone-B part, 0.97 to 1.11% under every numerator and denominator against 0.73 +- 0.073. The tone-A rate is not determined by these data, as the paper's 0.39% lies between the counts (0.27 to 0.81%), and even the 1 s filter gives only an upper bound, since a cue of 1 to 2 s cut short after 1 s still passes it. The result codes are undocumented, so the paper's counting may differ from all three.
deviations: The numerators are not in the claims file; they were counted from the definitions in the Results (Reaction time and tone discrimination, paragraph 2), from the L and R sensor series, with a recount keeping cue tones of at least 1 s (Behavioral task, cue 1000 to 2000 ms) and the result codes as variants.

outcomes.statement: Both L1 and R0 in the previous trial raise the left-choice probability (0.68 and 0.62), more after L1; both R1 and L0 lower it (0.30 and 0.39), more after R1. So rewarded experience modulates choice more than unrewarded experience.
outcomes.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 1; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: Both the experience L1 and R0 in the previous trial increased the probability of a left choice in the current trial [Fig. 2B, green arrow, P(L|L1) = 0.68; green arrowhead, P(L|R0) = 0.62]. The left choice probability after L1 was significantly higher than after R0 (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.0001) ... The left probability after R1 was significantly lower than after L0 [Fig. 2B, brown arrow, P(L|R1) = 0.30; brown arrowhead, P(L|L0) = 0.39] (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.0001)
outcomes.notes: Histories within blocks give P(L|L1) 0.678, P(L|R0) 0.617, P(L|R1) 0.300 and P(L|L0) 0.386; within sessions 0.680, 0.616, 0.299 and 0.388. All are in tolerance and in the stated order. The Mann-Whitney tests give p of 7.5e-19 and 4.0e-36 on trials and 3.8e-06 and 2.3e-06 on sessions (history within blocks), all below 0.0001. By rat, P(L|L1) exceeds P(L|R0) in four of six rats.

outcomes.statement: The experience two trials back still affects choice; P(L|R0 L1) = 0.66 differs from P(L|L1 L1) = 0.72.
outcomes.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 2; Figure 2B and 2C
outcomes.quote: the conditional probability P(L|R0 L1) = 0.66 (Fig. 2B,C, blue arrowhead), which is the probability of a left choice (at trial t) after R0 (at trial t − 2) and L1 (at trial t − 1), significantly differs from P(L|L1 L1) = 0.72 (Fig. 2B,C, blue arrow) ... (Mann– Whitney U test, p < 0.0001)
outcomes.notes: P(L|R0 L1) 0.663 and P(L|L1 L1) 0.718 with histories within blocks (0.661 and 0.721 within sessions), in the stated order and within tolerance. The Mann-Whitney test on the choices of the trials that follow each history (O8 a) gives p = 9.1e-07 and 5.9e-08; on per-session probabilities (O8 b) p = 0.032 and 0.012, which do not reach the paper's p < 0.0001. The criterion asks for p < 0.0001 under every reading, and the claims file blocks a claim whose method readings disagree. What the paper's tests rank is not stated (Results, History dependence, paragraphs 1 and 2); O8 (a) alone matches the paper's p = 0.94 for P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1) against P(L|R0 L1 L1 L1) (0.919 and 0.938 here, against 0.23 and 0.24 under O8 b). Asked of the paper's authors (findings).

outcomes.statement: Of the 128 mirror-paired four-trial sequences, L1 L1 L1 L1 (with R1 R1 R1 R1) is the most frequent (6.87%), R0 L1 L1 L1 (with L0 R1 R1 R1) the second (2.87%), R0 L0 R0 L0 (with L0 R0 L0 R0) the third (2.55%), and L0 L0 L0 L0 with R0 R0 R0 R0 make 1.28%.
outcomes.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraphs 2 and 3
outcomes.quote: the sequence L1 L1 L1 L1 and R1 R1 R1 R1 was observed most frequently (6.87% of all observed sequences of four trials). The sequence R0 L1 L1 L1 and L0 R1 R1 R1 was observed second most frequently (2.87%) ... The sequences R0 L0 R0 L0 and L0 R0 L0 R0 were observed third most frequently (2.55%) ... L0 L0 L0 L0 and R0 R0 R0 R0, which consisted of 1.28% of all observed sequences across the four trials
outcomes.notes: With a pair's percentage the sum of the two mirror sequences, the four pairs make 6.78, 2.94, 2.64 and 1.29% of 37,463 windows within blocks, and 6.88, 2.87, 2.54 and 1.28% of 38,965 windows within sessions; all are in tolerance and the first three pairs are the three most frequent, in order. The within-session values match the paper's to 0.01. Taking the mean of the two sequences gives half these values and does not match.

outcomes.statement: After repeated L1 the left-choice probability rises and converges near 0.75, and the effect of an earlier R0 fades under following L1s, so P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1) and P(L|R0 L1 L1 L1) do not differ (both 0.74).
outcomes.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: increased with the number of L1 experiences and converged around 0.75 ... There was no significant difference between P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1) = 0.74 and P(L|R0 L1 L1 L1) = 0.74 (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.94)
outcomes.notes: P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1) 0.734 and P(L|R0 L1 L1 L1) 0.736 (within sessions 0.743 and 0.741). The paper's test (O8 a) gives p = 0.919 and 0.938 (paper 0.94); O8 (b) gives 0.23 and 0.24. The left-choice probability rises from 0.678 (L1) to 0.718 (L1 L1) and 0.734 (L1 L1 L1 L1), within 0.075 of 0.75; P(L|L1 L1 L1) is 0.738.

outcomes.statement: After an unrewarded choice rats tended to choose the other action (switching), as seen in the alternating unrewarded sequences R0 L0 R0 L0 and L0 R0 L0 R0.
outcomes.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 3; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: These results illustrate that there was a “switching” behavior in which rats tended to choose the other action after one action was not rewarded
outcomes.notes: Under both history readings, after each prefix ending in L0 P(L) is 0.31 to 0.39, and after each ending in R0 it is 0.62 to 0.70; every 99% interval excludes 0.5.

outcomes.statement: After two or more unrewarded left choices the left-choice probability gradually rises, and P(L|L0 L0 L0) and P(L|L0 L0 L0 L0) are both above 0.5, so rats sometimes persevere after repeated non-reward.
outcomes.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 3; Figure 2E
outcomes.quote: The probability of a left choice gradually increased after two or more left choices with no reward. In particular, P(L|L0 L0 L0) and P(L|L0 L0 L0 L0) were both >0.5
outcomes.notes: P(L) after L0 L0, L0 L0 L0 and L0 L0 L0 L0 is 0.464, 0.575 and 0.698 within blocks (0.467, 0.574, 0.697 within sessions), rising, with the last two above 0.5. For the mirrored R0 sequence P(R) rises too (0.43, 0.45, 0.51), but P(R|R0 R0 R0) stays below 0.5; the criterion tests the left sequence.

outcomes.statement: Fitted by least squares to the six four-trial sequences of Fig. 2C and 2D, the local matching law and standard Q-learning cannot represent switching, while F-Q and DF-Q can; the averaged residual errors are 0.0102, 0.0073, 0.0010 and 0.0002.
outcomes.source: Results, Modeling rats' strategies with a reinforcement learning model, paragraph 3; Figure 3; Table 1
outcomes.quote: The results showed that the local matching law (Fig. 3A) and the standard Q-learning model (Fig. 3B) were not able to represent switching behavior, whereas the F-Q- and DF-Q-learning models were (Fig. 3C,D). The averaged residual errors of the local matching law, the standard Q, F-Q, and DF-Q models were 0.0102, 0.0073, 0.0010, and 0.0002, respectively
outcomes.notes: Under all eight readings (O7, O1, residual) the residuals are in the order local matching (0.0099 to 0.0102) > standard Q (0.0071 to 0.0073) > F-Q (0.00079 to 0.00102) > DF-Q (0.00011 to 0.00027), and switching is represented by F-Q and DF-Q but not by the local matching law or standard Q. The DF-Q residual is outside its tolerance (0.0002 +- 0.00002) under every reading and F-Q is outside under the 12-point reading, so the order and switching hold and some values do not. The local matching law's optimum is alpha 0, a constant 0.5.
deviations: Fitted with L-BFGS-B from a grid of starting points under the bounds alpha in [0, 1], kappa1 in [0, 10], kappa2 in [-10, 10] and Q0 in [0, 10]; the paper names no optimizer or bounds (a standard choice).

outcomes.statement: The least-squares fits give the parameters of Table 1 (alpha1, alpha2, kappa1, kappa2, Q0) for each model.
outcomes.source: Table 1
outcomes.inferred: Numbers only in Table 1; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: Under O1 (a) 8 of 14 values are within tolerance (6 under O1 b), fewer than the 10 needed for partial reproduction. F-Q alpha, kappa1 and kappa2 and all five DF-Q values match; standard Q (alpha 0.30 to 0.32, kappa1 2.71 to 2.85, Q0 1.24 to 1.29), F-Q Q0 and the local matching law (alpha 0 and Q0 0, against 0.05 and 0.07) do not. With alpha1 = alpha2 the initial value cancels from QL - QR, so the F-Q Q0 is not determined by the fit (0.05 to 1.0 here); the paper's 0.00 is one of many equal optima. Under O1 (a) the paper's own Table 1 values give nearly the fitted residual (mean over 24 points, O7 a: local matching law 0.0103 against 0.0102 at alpha 0.05 and Q0 0.07, standard Q 0.00722 against 0.00720, F-Q equal, DF-Q 0.00028 against 0.00027), so the surface is flat and the paper's values lie near the optimum; under O1 (b) they are far worse (0.018 to 0.044 for all but F-Q).

outcomes.statement: The first- to fourth-order Markov models reach normalized likelihoods of 0.528, 0.532, 0.534 and 0.532 on test data; the third order is best and the fourth is lower, presumably by overfitting its 256 parameters.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "Figure 5 shows"; Figure 5
outcomes.quote: The normalized likelihood of the first-order Markov model was 0.528 ... The normalized likelihood for the second- and third-order Markov models increased to 0.532 and 0.534, respectively ... The performance of the fourth-order model was 0.532, lower than that of the third-order model
outcomes.notes: With the split by alternate sessions (O3 a) the four orders score 0.5283, 0.5318, 0.5336 and 0.5319, with order 3 highest and order 4 lower; O3 (b) gives the same order. The random split (O3 c) gives values in tolerance but order 4 (0.5334) above order 3 (0.5332). The criterion asks for the result under every reading of the split, and the readings disagree. O3 (a) is the only reading whose training set holds the paper's 19,986 choice trials (test 19,189 against 19,186). Both O6 readings agree. Asked of the paper's authors (findings).

outcomes.statement: With constant parameters, standard Q, F-Q and DF-Q (0.527, 0.531, 0.531) predict much better than the local matching law (0.508), but worse than the first- or second-order Markov models.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "Predictions by the standard Q-"; Figure 5; Table 2
outcomes.quote: Predictions by the standard Q-, F-Q-, and DF-Q-learning models with constant parameters (α and κ) were much better (0.527, 0.531, and 0.531, respectively) than the predictions of the local matching law (0.508), but poorer than that of the first- or second-order Markov models
outcomes.notes: In every reading standard Q, F-Q and DF-Q (constant) score 0.5240 to 0.5267, 0.5280 to 0.5308 and 0.5283 to 0.5306, within tolerance, above the local matching law. The local matching law with Qi(1) = 0, as the Methods and the criterion give it, predicts 0/0 at the first trial and probability 1 after the first reward on one side; fitted, its optimum is alpha 0, a constant 0.5, and it scores 0.500 under O1 (a) and less under O1 (b), out of tolerance. With an initial value the paper does not give (0.1, 0.5 or 1.0) it scores 0.504 to 0.508 under O1 (a), in tolerance, and 0.491 to 0.502 under O1 (b). The measured local matching law value (0.5064) is the one under the assumed Qi(1) = 0.5; under Qi(1) = 0 it is 0.5000. The paper's 0.508 cannot come from the model as specified, so its procedure is not fixed. F-Q and DF-Q (constant) exceed the first-order Markov model, as the paper's numbers do (not part of the outcome). Asked of the paper's authors (findings).
deviations: Constant fits use L-BFGS-B (O4 b) and the best point of a 0.05 grid within 3 steps of it in every parameter (O4 a); a full four-parameter grid was not run.

outcomes.statement: With time-varying parameters standard Q, F-Q and DF-Q improve to 0.5304, 0.5375 and 0.5368, and F-Q with time-varying parameters predicts best of all models.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "With time-varying parameters"; Figure 5
outcomes.quote: With time-varying parameters, the performance of the standard Q, F-Q, and DF-Q models improved (0.5304, 0.5375, and 0.5368, respectively). The F-Q-learning model with time-varying parameters produced the best prediction performance
outcomes.notes: In all 48 readings the three time-varying models are in tolerance and each beats its constant version; the main reading gives 0.5304, 0.5374 and 0.5369 (paper 0.5304, 0.5375, 0.5368). F-Q (variable) is the best model in 40 readings; in 8 of the 12 with O1 (b) and clipped drift (O5 b), those on splits (a) and (b), DF-Q (variable) leads it by at most 0.0002 (on split c F-Q leads), so the criterion's partial rule (F-Q or DF-Q highest, values in tolerance, F-Q not always first) holds under every reading. On split (a) the average of six filter seeds keeps the order (F-Q 0.53752 against DF-Q 0.53710 under O1 a, O5 a; DF-Q 0.53481 against 0.53468 under O1 b, O5 b). A 5000-particle sigma search on a wider grid (split a, O1 a) gives F-Q 0.5372 and DF-Q 0.5372 under O5 (a), 0.5374 and 0.5373 under O5 (b); the paper's Table 2 sigmas give 0.5376 and 0.5369 in the main reading. The claim depends on fig5-markov-accuracy and fig5-constant-models, which are blocked for details this claim does not use (the Markov order 3 against 4 under one split, the local matching law's initial value); F-Q and DF-Q (variable) exceed every Markov and local-matching score under every reading, so the claim is tested.
deviations: The outcome reads the criterion's partial rule as holding when its condition (F-Q or DF-Q variable highest, values in tolerance) holds under every reading, although in 40 readings F-Q is first, which alone would give reproduced. The claims file's general rule blocks a claim whose readings give different outcomes; this reading was assumed as the partial rule is written for the case where F-Q is not first under every reading.

The sigma search ran with 1000 particles on a 4 x 4 grid holding the Table 2 values; the chosen sigmas were then run with 5000 particles. A 5000-particle search on a 6 x 5 grid (sigma_alpha 0.0025 to 0.08, sigma_kappa 0.025 to 0.15) was run for split (a) and O1 (a) as a check.
Systematic resampling in the particle filter (a standard choice for the offspring numbers the supplement describes).

outcomes.statement: Per test session, the F-Q and DF-Q models with time-varying parameters predict significantly better than every other model, including the third-order Markov model.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "A statistical test"; Figure 5 legend
outcomes.quote: the prediction accuracies of both the F-Q- and DF-Q-learning models with time-varying parameters were significantly higher than those of all other models (paired-sample Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p < 0.05 for third Markov model, p < 0.01 for other models)

statistics.about: F-Q and DF-Q (variable) against the third-order Markov model
F-Q and DF-Q (variable) against the other models

outcomes.notes: In the main reading (O3 a, O1 a, O5 a) 15 of 18 comparisons meet the paper's levels. F-Q (variable) against DF-Q (constant) gives p = 0.036 (needs 0.01); DF-Q (variable) against standard Q (variable) p = 0.030 and against DF-Q (constant) p = 0.073. Both beat the third-order Markov model (p = 0.0067 and 0.014, two-sided). With the six-seed average of the filter these three p are 0.034, 0.026 and 0.073, and over the six seeds 0.036 to 0.044, 0.027 to 0.040 and 0.073 to 0.090, so filter noise does not decide them. All 18 pass two-sided in 2 of 48 readings (split b, O1 a, O5 a) and one-sided in 8; the partial condition holds in some readings and not others, and under O1 (b) only 4 to 8 pass. The readings give different outcomes. Against the local matching law p < 1e-9 under every initial value.

outcomes.statement: The F-Q and DF-Q models with time-varying parameters do not differ in prediction accuracy (p = 0.067), so F-Q, with fewer parameters, is regarded as the better model.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "A statistical test"
outcomes.quote: There was no significant difference between these two models (paired-sample Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p = 0.067)
outcomes.notes: In the main reading the two-sided paired Wilcoxon test finds F-Q (variable) better than DF-Q (variable), p = 0.0082, 27 of 35 sessions, median difference 0.00064 (one-sided 0.0041). In 4 of 12 readings the test finds a difference and in 8 it does not (p 0.058 to 0.70). Filter noise does not explain the split: on split (a) with O1 (a) each of six seeds finds a difference (p 0.0053 to 0.039 under O5 a, 0.0030 to 0.030 under O5 b; six-seed average 0.017 and 0.0091), and with O1 (b) none does (p 0.13 to 0.98). The readings disagree.

outcomes.statement: Taking left when the predicted P(L) exceeds 0.5 and right otherwise, the best model predicts 68% of choices correctly, averaged over the 35 test sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "With time-varying parameters"
outcomes.quote: If we take binary predictions from the choice probability [left for PL(t) > 0.5, right for PL(t) < 0.5], the average percentage of correct predictions over 35 test sessions is 68%
outcomes.notes: F-Q (variable) predicts 67.7% of test choices correctly on average in the main reading (sessions 60.7 to 77.2%), and 67.0 to 68.0% across the 12 readings.

outcomes.statement: The maximum-likelihood parameters on the training data are those of Table 2 (for example F-Q constant alpha 0.55, kappa1 1.25, kappa2 0.55; F-Q variable sigma_alpha 0.005, sigma_kappa 0.07).
outcomes.source: Table 2
outcomes.inferred: Numbers only in Table 2; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: In the main reading 8 of 16 values are within 10%; other readings of O3 to O5 under O1 (a) give 6 to 8, and O1 (b) gives 0 to 4, so the 8 needed for partial reproduction is not reached under every reading of O3 to O5. Standard Q kappa1, F-Q alpha1, kappa1 and kappa2, the local matching law's alpha (with Qi(1) = 0.5; 0 with Qi(1) = 0) and three of six sigmas match in the main reading. The DF-Q constant optimum on the split-a training data is alpha1 0.45, alpha2 0.05, kappa1 2.25, kappa2 -1.1, with a training normalized likelihood 0.00029 above that at Table 2's values, a different optimum; on splits b and c the paper's values are within 0.0002 of the optimum. Under O1 (b) Table 2's values are 0.010 to 0.027 below the optimum for every Q model. The sigma surface is flat: with 5000 particles on a wider grid (split a, O1 a) the best sigmas are standard Q (0.02, 0.07), F-Q (0.02, 0.025), DF-Q (0.01, 0.025) under O5 (a) and (0.04, 0.15), (0.08, 0.07), (0.04, 0.05) under O5 (b), the last two at or near the grid's edge. Table 2's F-Q and DF-Q sigmas are within 0.0005 of the best training score under O5 (a); under O5 (b) F-Q's are 0.0008 below and DF-Q's 0.0002. The local matching law alpha matches only with the initial value Qi(1) = 0.5, which the paper does not give; with the Methods' Qi(1) = 0 the main reading has 7 of 16, and the outcome is the same. Under O5 (a) one grid point (standard Q, 0.02 and 0.10) collapsed the filter in one session (score 0.398 over the training sessions).
deviations: The 1000-particle sigma search of fig5-variable-models-best gives the sigmas compared; a 5000-particle search on a wider grid is shown as a check for split (a) and O1 (a).

outcomes.statement: Across all data the time-varying estimates average, for F-Q, alpha1 0.47 ± 0.25, kappa1 1.61 ± 0.77, kappa2 1.10 ± 0.87, and for DF-Q, alpha1 0.45 ± 0.19, alpha2 0.46 ± 0.19, kappa1 1.69 ± 0.77, kappa2 1.24 ± 0.92; standard Q alpha1 0.45 ± 0.23, kappa1 1.86 ± 0.68.
outcomes.source: Table 3
outcomes.inferred: Numbers only in Table 3; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: With the Table 2 sigmas and O1 (a), all nine means are within tolerance in all 8 readings of O5, O13 and the averaging (pooled trials and O13 a, standard Q 0.45 +- 0.25 and 1.83 +- 0.85, F-Q 0.48 +- 0.27, 1.64 +- 0.79 and 1.19 +- 0.82, DF-Q 0.47 +- 0.24, 0.51 +- 0.27, 1.72 +- 0.78 and 1.26 +- 0.86). Under O1 (b) 6 of 9 means match, the three kappa1 means about half the paper's. The criterion asks for every O1 reading and the readings disagree. The table 1 and 2 criteria treat O1 as the parameterization of the reported values, under which O1 (a) would be the match; this is asked of a reader (questions/001641.yaml).

outcomes.statement: With time-varying parameters, F-Q and DF-Q capture win-stay-lose-switch behaviour by raising kappa2 close to kappa1, and persevering behaviour by a negative kappa2, which the standard Q model cannot.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraphs beginning "Figure 4A–F" and "Figure 4, B, D, and F"; Figure 4
outcomes.quote: This behavior was captured by the F-Q- and DF-Q-learning models, with both models showing an increase in the nonreward aversion parameter κ2 close to the reward reinforcement parameter κ1 ... The F-Q and DF-Q models captured this behavior by exhibiting a negative value for the aversion parameter κ2 (Fig. 4H)
outcomes.notes: In all 24 readings (O1, O5, O13, run length 5, 10, 15) some win-stay-lose-switch episode ends with F-Q kappa2 within 25% of kappa1 (22 to 728 such episodes of 75 to 2374), some persevering episode ends with kappa2 below 0 (4 to 82 of 4 to 131), and over the episodes F-Q (variable) has the higher mean per-trial likelihood (0.62 to 0.74 against 0.59 to 0.68 for standard Q).
deviations: Runs use the Table 2 sigmas; the representative sessions of Fig. 4 are not identified.

outcomes.statement: The actual left-choice probability, plotted against QL - QR from the standard Q, F-Q and DF-Q models, confirms that the models' predictions are meaningful.
outcomes.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "With time-varying parameters"; supplemental Data 1 (not available)
outcomes.quote: the meaningful performances of the standard Q, F-Q, and DF-Q models were also conformed by plotting the actual left-choice probability for the difference between QL and QR (supplemental Data 1
outcomes.notes: For all 12 readings (variable and constant versions, three models, two update forms) the left-choice fraction rises over ten equal-count bins of QL - QR, Spearman 1.0, from 0.22 to 0.24 in the lowest bin to 0.73 to 0.78 in the highest.

outcomes.statement: Analysis used 148 NAc neurons and 66 VP neurons from six rats in 70 sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal recording data, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Subsequent analysis was performed for a total of 148 NAc neurons and 66 VP neurons from six rats during 70 sessions
outcomes.notes: 148 NAc and 66 VP units, from six rats, in 52 of 70 sessions; 18 files have no units table. Rat 44 contributes one unit and rat 35 none in the VP.

outcomes.statement: VP neurons fire faster than NAc neurons during the task (10.2 ± 9.1 against 2.6 ± 2.6 Hz, mean ± SD).
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: VP neurons showed a higher firing rate than NAc neurons overall. The average and SD of the firing rate of VP neurons and NAc neurons during the task were 10.2±9.1 and 2.6±2.6 Hz, respectively
outcomes.notes: Over the whole recording (O15 a) VP 10.21 +- 9.14 Hz and NAc 2.60 +- 2.59 Hz; over the trials (O15 b) 10.21 +- 9.15 and 2.62 +- 2.61 Hz. Means and SDs are within tolerance and VP is faster in every rat with VP units.
deviations: The files give no recording span; reading O15 (a) takes the session's first to last spike or trial event.

outcomes.statement: After cue onset (phase 2), 54% of NAc neurons (80 of 148) and 50% of VP neurons (33 of 66) fire differently for the choice and the no-choice tone (state-coding neurons).
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: After the onset of the cue tone (phase 2), 54% (80 of 148) of NAc neurons and 50% (33 of 66) of VP neurons showed different firing patterns in response to the choice tone and the no-choice tone
outcomes.notes: With successful choice and no-choice trials (O14 a) 80 of 148 NAc and 33 of 66 VP units, exactly as reported. With all tone-A and tone-B trials (O14 b) 83 and 37; 37 is outside the VP tolerance. The criterion asks for every reading and they disagree. O14 (a) follows the Methods' comparison of "choice trials and no-choice trials" (Comparison of perievent time histograms), which the Behavioral task defines as successful trials, but the paper does not say that error trials were left out. Asked of the paper's authors (findings).

outcomes.statement: By block comparison of firing, few neurons code an action value; QL-coding neurons are 6, 8 and 7% of NAc neurons and 11, 18 and 21% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3, and QR-coding neurons 7, 8 and 5% (NAc) and 11, 9 and 11% (VP).
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B; Figure 7E and 7F
outcomes.quote: Before the onset of the nose poke action at the center hole (phase 1), the percentage of QL-coding neurons in the NAc was 6% (9 of 148), and 11% (7 of 66) in the VP ... The percentage of QR-coding neurons in the NAc was 7% (11 of 148), and 11% (7 of 66) in the VP ... The percentage of QL-coding neurons in the NAc was 8% (12 of 148) and 18% (12 of 66) in the VP. The percentage of QR-coding neurons in the NAc was 8% (12 of 148) and 9% (6 of 66) in the VP. Before the initiation of action (phase 3), QL-coding neurons represented 7% (11 of 148) of the neurons in the NAc and 21% (14 of 66) of those in the VP. QR-coding neurons represented 5% (8 of 148) of the neurons in the NAc and 11% (7 of 66) of those in the VP
outcomes.notes: 9 of 12 counts are within 2 neurons; all populations are under 25% of their region (largest 19.7%). NAc QL in phases 1 and 2 (13 and 15 against 9 and 12) and NAc QR in phase 1 (16 against 11) are higher.
deviations: The last 20 choice trials of every block were used, including a session's last, unfinished block; the paper does not say whether it was included.

outcomes.statement: Before action initiation (phase 3), 11% of NAc neurons (17 of 148) and 18% of VP neurons (12 of 66) code the action to be chosen (action command-coding neurons).
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: Neurons encoding the action to be chosen before execution represented 11% (17 of 148) of the neurons in the NAc and 18% (12 of 66) of those in the VP (action command-coding neurons)
outcomes.notes: 15 of 148 NAc units (expected 17, tolerance 1.7) and 14 of 66 VP units (expected 12, tolerance 1.2) code the upcoming action in phase 3. Each count is 2 from the expected one, NAc below and VP above.

outcomes.statement: After action onset (phase 4), 41% of NAc neurons (61 of 148) and 39% of VP neurons (26 of 66) code the selected action.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: After the action onset (phase 4), the proportion of action-coding neurons increased to 41% (61 of 148) in the NAc and 39% (26 of 66) in the VP
outcomes.notes: 63 of 148 NAc and 26 of 66 VP units code the chosen action in phase 4 (expected 61 and 26).

outcomes.statement: After the reward or no-reward tone (phase 5), 63% of NAc neurons (93 of 148) and 68% of VP neurons (45 of 66) code reward availability.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: After the onset of the reward tone or no-reward tone (phase 5), 63% (93 of 148) of NAc neurons and 68% (45 of 66) of VP neurons coded reward availability
outcomes.notes: 96 of 148 NAc and 44 of 66 VP units code reward in phase 5 (expected 93 and 45). The no-reward tone onset was found for all but 695 unit-trials (30 units), whose phase-5 count is missing.
deviations: Phase 5 starts at the reward tone onset or at the onset of a short (under 1.5 s) tone in the SpTone Err series within 1 s after L or R entry, as the no-reward tone is stored there.

outcomes.statement: The NAc and VP do not differ in the percentages of neurons coding trial type, action command, chosen action and reward outcome.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 5; Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: Comparison of the percentages of coding neurons in the NAc and VP revealed no differences with trial type, action command, chosen action, and reward outcome (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.59, p = 0.19, p = 0.80, and p = 0.45, respectively)
outcomes.notes: The test as O9 reads it reproduces the paper's p-values from the paper's counts (0.031, 0.0038, 0.58). On this dataset it finds no difference for state (54.1% against 50.0%, p = 0.58), action (42.6% against 39.4%, p = 0.66) or reward (64.9% against 66.7%, p = 0.80), but finds one for action command (10.1% NAc against 21.2% VP, p = 0.029; paper p = 0.19).

outcomes.statement: QL-coding neurons are a larger share of VP than of NAc neurons after cue onset (phase 2) and before action initiation (phase 3).
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 5; Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: Surprisingly, the percentages of QL-coding neurons both after cue onset (phase 2) and before action initiation (phase 3) were significantly higher in the VP than in the NAc (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.03 < 0.05, p = 0.004 < 0.01, respectively)
outcomes.notes: Phase 3, VP 19.7% against NAc 7.4%, p = 0.0088; phase 2, VP 16.7% against NAc 10.1%, p = 0.18. The VP share is higher in both but significant only in phase 3.

outcomes.statement: QR-coding neurons do not differ in share between the VP and NAc in phases 2 and 3.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 5; Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: whereas those of QR-coding neurons were not significantly different between areas at the two different times (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.81, and 0.17)
outcomes.notes: Phase 2, NAc 8.1% and VP 12.1% (difference 4.0 points, p = 0.35); phase 3, 6.8% and 12.1% (5.4 points, p = 0.19). Neither finds a difference.

outcomes.statement: Among state-coding neurons (48% NAc, 36% VP preferring tone A), action command-coding neurons (53%, 50% preferring left) and action-coding neurons (57%, 50% preferring left), the share with each preference does not differ from 50%.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 6
outcomes.quote: Of the state-coding neurons, 48% (38 of 80) in the NAc and 36% (12 of 33) in the VP showed a greater response to tone A than to tone B. Of the action command-coding neurons, 53% (9 of 17) in the NAc and 50% (6 of 12) in the VP showed greater activity in left-selected trials than in right-selected trials. In the action-coding neurons, 57% (35 of 61) in the NAc and 50% (13 of 26) in the VP showed greater activity in left-selected than in right-selected trials. All of these populations were not significantly different from 50% (Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p > 0.05)
outcomes.notes: No signed-rank test (O11 a, p 0.43 to 0.90) or sign test (O11 b, p 0.16 to 1.0) finds a departure from 50%. Five of six percentages are within tolerance; NAc action command is 46.7% (7 of 15) against 53%.

outcomes.statement: 73% of NAc reward-coding neurons (68 of 93) respond more to the no-reward than to the reward tone, more than the 50% of chance, while the VP share (56%, 25 of 45) does not differ from 50%.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 6
outcomes.quote: However, 73% (68 of 93) of the reward-coding neurons in the NAc showed a larger response to the no-reward than to the reward tone. This percentage of cells was significantly larger than the 50% predicted by chance (Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p < 0.0001). The percentage of reward-coding neurons in the VP (56%; 25 of 45), however, was not significantly different from 50% (Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p > 0.05)
outcomes.notes: 70 of 96 NAc reward-coding units (72.9%) respond more to the no-reward tone. The sign test (O11 b) gives p = 8e-06, but the signed-rank test of the differences (O11 a) gives p = 0.0032, above the paper's p < 0.0001, so the NAc part fails under one reading. The VP part holds, 23 of 44 (52.3%), signed-rank p = 0.30.

outcomes.statement: Splitting NAc neurons into tentative core and shell groups by electrode position, the same analyses find no difference between core and shell neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 7; supplemental Data 3 (not available)
outcomes.quote: The same analysis described above found no significant differences between core and shell neurons (supplemental Data 3
outcomes.notes: Units are labelled NAc or VP only. The files give no core or shell assignment, no bundle coordinates and no per-session depth, so the NAc units cannot be split as the paper's Fig. 6 does. The archive's metadata and the electrode table (location NAc or VP) were checked.

outcomes.statement: By regression on the block reward probabilities, QL-coding neurons are 9, 10 and 7% of NAc neurons and 15, 24 and 26% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3, and QR-coding neurons 11, 9 and 6% (NAc) and 9, 17 and 14% (VP).
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8C
outcomes.quote: QL-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to QL (t test, p < 0.01) but not to QR, were present in percentages of 9, 10, and 7% in the NAc, and 15, 24, and 26% in the VP for different time bins (Fig. 8A, phases 1–3) ... QR-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to QR (t test, p < 0.01) but not to QL, were present in percentages of 11, 9, and 6% in the NAc, and 9, 17, and 14% in the VP
outcomes.notes: 6 of 12 percentages within tolerance, fewer than the 9 needed for partial reproduction. NAc QL is higher than reported in all three phases (12.2, 11.5, 9.5% against 9, 10, 7%), as are VP QL in phase 1 and NAc QR in phase 3; VP QR in phase 2 is lower (13.6 against 17%). One unit had no variance in its last-20 counts and was counted as not coding.

outcomes.statement: In the regression analysis, QL-coding neurons are a larger share of VP than of NAc neurons in phases 2 and 3.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8C
outcomes.quote: In phases 2 and 3, there were significant differences in the size of the population of QL-coding neurons in the NAc, and in the VP (p = 0.007 and 0.0001 < 0.01, Mann–Whitney U test)
outcomes.notes: VP against NAc QL share 25.8% against 11.5% in phase 2 (p = 0.0085) and 24.2% against 9.5% in phase 3 (p = 0.0041), both p < 0.01 (paper 0.007 and 0.0001).

outcomes.statement: Regression detects slightly more action value-coding neurons (Fig. 8C) than the block comparison (Fig. 8B), and the two are consistent.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8
outcomes.quote: These regression analysis results were consistent with those obtained by comparing the perievent time histograms (Fig. 8B). However, the number of the detected action value-coding neurons was slightly larger in Figure 8C than in Figure 8B
outcomes.notes: Regression 165 QL- and QR-coding units over phases and regions, block comparison 133 (paper about 146 and 116). The VP has the larger QL share in phases 2 and 3 in both analyses.

outcomes.statement: State value-coding neurons are 12, 8 and 8% of NAc neurons and 18, 20 and 20% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3, with the VP share larger in phases 2 and 3.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8D
outcomes.quote: State value-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to [QL(t) + QR(t)] but not to [QL(t) − QR(t)], were present in percentages of 12, 8, and 8% in the NAc, and 18, 20, and 20% in the VP (Fig. 8D). In phases 2 and 3, these differences between the sizes of the populations in the NAc and VP were significant (p = 0.02 and 0.02 < 0.05, respectively; Mann–Whitney U test)
outcomes.notes: 2 of 6 percentages match (NAc phase 1, VP phase 3). The VP share is higher than the NAc's in phases 2 and 3 (13.6 against 10.8%, 19.7 against 10.8%) but not significantly (p = 0.55 and 0.080).

outcomes.statement: Policy-coding neurons are 10, 9 and 7% of NAc neurons and 11, 15 and 14% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8D
outcomes.quote: Policy-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to [QL(t) − QR(t)] but not to [QL(t) + QR(t)], were present in percentages of 10, 9, and 7% in the NAc, and 11, 15, and 14% in the VP (Fig. 8D)
outcomes.notes: 5 of 6 percentages match; NAc phase 1 is 7.4% against 10% (outside 2 neurons).

outcomes.statement: Every coding population of Figure 8 is larger than expected by chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8 legend
outcomes.quote: All percentages shown in Figure 8 were significantly larger than those predicted by chance (p < 0.01, binomial test)
outcomes.notes: All 44 populations of Fig. 8B to 8D give p < 0.01 under both chance levels (largest p 4.7e-06).

outcomes.statement: Information about the trial type (state) in the NAc and VP rises right after cue onset and again after center-hole exit.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 9; Figure 9A and 9B
outcomes.quote: The information coding state in the NAc and VP (green lines) increased immediately after the onset of the cue tone, and again after exiting from the center hole
outcomes.notes: In all 12 readings (window placement, random events) and both regions, state MI within 0.5 s after cue onset (0.030 to 0.057 bits/s) is above threshold and above the 0.5 s before (0.0003 to 0.027), and the exit-aligned curve has a later local maximum above threshold (0.108 to 0.121 bits/s at 0.8 to 2.1 s) exceeding its value at the exit (0.033 to 0.040).
deviations: Time ranges of the curves (-1 to 3 s from cue onset, -2 to 4 s from center exit) are a standard choice; the paper's figure, not readable here, sets its own.

outcomes.statement: Information about the chosen action is very weak before center-hole exit, rises rapidly after it, and peaks around entry to the L or R hole.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 9; Figure 9B
outcomes.quote: Information related to action choice was very weak in both the NAc and VP before the onset of the choice (before the exit of the center hole), but increased rapidly after the choice onset, and showed a peak around the time of entry to the left or right hole
outcomes.notes: Action MI before center exit averages 0.003 to 0.009 bits/s, under a fifth of the peak (0.048 to 0.059), and peaks 0.3 to 1.1 s after exit, within 0.5 s of the median reaction time (0.754 s), in all readings and both regions.

outcomes.statement: Information about reward rises when the reward or no-reward tone is presented at L or R entry, then decreases gradually but lasts until the next trial.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 9; Figure 9B; Discussion, Information coding in NAc and VP, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Information related to the reward started to increase at the presentation of reward/no-reward tone, which was presented at the time of entry to the left or right hole. The reward information gradually decreased, but was sustained until the subsequent trial
outcomes.notes: Reward MI peaks at 0.093 (NAc) and 0.106 (VP) bits/s 1.3 to 1.9 s after center exit, decreases, and the previous trial's reward is above threshold around the next cue onset (0.015 to 0.019 bits/s) in all readings. Before the median L or R entry it is low but above threshold in 16 to 28 of 23 to 28 windows (up to 0.0044 NAc and 0.0070 VP against thresholds up to 0.0023 and 0.0033); aligned to each trial's own entry, 12 to 21 of 16 to 21 windows before entry are above threshold (up to 0.0063 and 0.0067 bits/s, 5.6 to 6.7% of the peak). The criterion's condition below threshold before entry fails in every reading and the criterion gives no partial rule. Whether the paper says this is asked of a reader (questions/001641.yaml): it says reward information started to increase at the tone and lasted into the next trial, which would allow some information before entry.

outcomes.statement: Information about the action values QL and QR is above the significance threshold in the NAc and VP but low and without clear peaks, while state, action and reward information are robust.
outcomes.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 10; Figure 9; Discussion, Information coding in NAc and VP, last paragraph but one
outcomes.quote: Information regarding action values QL and QR in the NAc and VP were found to be larger than the threshold values, indicating a significant level of information (p < 0.01) (see Materials and Methods). However, this level of information was still relatively low and without clear peaks, whereas information about state, action, and reward was robustly represented in the NAc and VP
outcomes.notes: Across the four F-Q runs (O1 and O5, Table 2 sigmas) and all 192 readings, QL and QR MI exceed the threshold in every window and peak at up to 0.042 bits/s, under the peaks of state, action and reward MI (0.108 to 0.121). With the predictive mean (O13 a) the curves are flat in all 96 readings (maximum at most 1.76 times the median in the O1 a, O5 a run). With the posterior mean after e(t) (O13 b), which now includes trial t's choice and reward (corrected after verification), the largest maximum per run is 2.4 to 3.4 times the median and flatness fails in 48 of 96 readings. The comparison with the other events holds in every reading, the criterion's partial rule.
deviations: The outcome reads the criterion's partial rule as holding when its condition (the comparison with the other events) holds under every reading, although under O13 (a) all parts hold, which alone would give reproduced. The claims file's general rule blocks a claim whose readings give different outcomes; this reading was assumed, as for fig5-variable-models-best.
The O13 (b) estimate is the mean of the resampled particles after the Q update with a(t) and r(t), before the parameters drift.

outcomes.statement: Information about the chosen action in the NAc and VP lasts beyond the peak of reward information.
outcomes.source: Discussion, Information coding in NAc and VP, paragraph 3; Figure 9
outcomes.quote: In particular, we showed that a representation of information regarding action in the NAc and VP lasted beyond the peak of information regarding reward (Fig. 9)
outcomes.notes: At the reward MI peak (1.3 to 1.9 s after exit) action MI is 0.027 to 0.032 bits/s and 0.5 s later 0.019 to 0.026, above thresholds of at most 0.0027, in all readings and both regions.

findings.statement: The trial table's `result` column says "Refer to the Discription in 'Result' column", but no such description is in the files. Codes 1 to 5 occur (33,243, 8084, 18,639, 141 and 104 trials). Codes 1 and 3 can be read from the other columns (rewarded or successful, and unrewarded choice); the error codes 2, 4 and 5 cannot be told apart with certainty, so the paper's error rates (0.39% and 0.73%) could not be recounted with certainty; the tone-A rate is not determined (0.27 to 0.81% under different counts), while every count of the tone-B rate gives 0.97 to 1.11%.

The no-reward tone of choice trials (500 Hz, 250 ms) is stored in the `SpTone Err` and `ViTone Err` series, named as the error tone, together with the error tone; the two are told apart only by their duration (about 0.3 s and 2 s).
The error tone lasts about 2 s in the event series (8299 tones over 1.5 s), where the paper's Behavioral task gives 1000 ms.

Units carry only `Area` (NAc or VP) and an electrode number. The NAc core and shell assignment the paper uses (Fig. 6, supplemental Data 3), the bundle positions and the per-session depth are not in the dataset.

18 of the 70 files have no units table (11 of the 12 sessions of rat 44, and seven others); the files do not say whether no unit was recorded or none was accepted in these sessions. Units in the other 52 sessions match the paper's counts (148 NAc, 66 VP).
Three choice trials have an L or R entry time before the center-hole exit (reaction times of -19,829, -11,554 and -5.2 s), and one error trial has no `state`.

The cue tone probably stops when the rat leaves the center hole early. Some tone-A tones in the event series last under 1 s (1st percentile 0.46 s), against the task's 1000 to 2000 ms, and 96 of the 317 tone-A error trials with no L or R entry have a cue under 1 s (1st percentile 0.12 s), while the trials with result codes 5 and 4 have full-length cues (1st percentile 1.05 and 1.03 s). In the 96 short-tone trials the center exit falls within 10 ms of the trial table's tone offset (5th to 95th percentile -0.010 to -0.003 s), as it does in most trials with a full cue, so early exits cannot be told from held cues by the exit time. Cue duration marks only exits before 1 s, as a cue of 1 to 2 s cut short after 1 s looks like a full one. The files do not describe this.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebook of the first run with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier tested class_index, mi_bias_corrected, q_update, count_spikes and mw_indicator_p on synthetic inputs, ran the particle filter over four seeds on synthetic F-Q data, and range-read the electrode tables of two files for the core and shell check. Its report gave its own outcome for each claim; 36 of 46 agree with the record as it was. Report in transcripts/001641/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: Cell 22: both values and the direction match. O8 (a) gives p about 1e-6, but O8 (b) gives p = 0.032 and 0.012, not < 0.0001. The readings disagree (methods_underspecified).

Cell 41: all values are within 0.005 under every reading, and order 3 is highest under O3 (a) and (b). Under O3 (c), order 4 (0.5334) beats order 3 (0.5332). O3 (a) gives exactly the paper's 19,986 training trials. Blocked (methods_underspecified).

Cell 43: Q, F-Q and DF-Q are within tolerance and above the local matching law under every reading. With Qi(1) = 0, as the criterion fixes, the local matching law scores 0.500 (O1 a) or 0.41 to 0.43 (O1 b), out of tolerance; it reaches 0.506 to 0.507 only with the author's assumed Qi(1) of 0.1 to 1.0, and only under O1 (a). As the paper specifies it, the model is degenerate (problem 3: the headline row and the Wilcoxon inputs use Qi(1) = 0.5, so the main table reads as if the local matching law were reproduced). Blocked (methods_underspecified).

Cell 45: all three values are within tolerance and above their constant versions in 48 of 48 readings. F-Q is best in 40 readings; DF-Q is best in 8 (O1 b, O5 b, splits a and b). Problem 1: each 5000-particle run uses one seed, and on synthetic data the seed noise is about the size of the F-Q and DF-Q differences. Problem 2: the sigma search used 1000 particles on a 4 x 4 grid with sigma_alpha at the grid maximum. It asked for scores over several seeds, the test scores at the paper's Table 2 sigmas and a 5000-particle search past sigma_alpha 0.02.

Cell 47: all 18 comparisons pass only under O3 (b), O1 (a), O5 (a). Under split (a), the paper's split, they fail; for example DF-Q (variable) against DF-Q (constant) gives two-sided p = 0.073. Blocked (methods_underspecified). Problem 10: the partial column is computed two-sided only; one-sided, the main reading would meet the partial condition. It asked for the local matching law comparisons under the other Qi(1) values.

Cell 48: two-sided p < 0.05 in 4 of 12 readings, including the main one (O3 a, O1 a, O5 a: p = 0.008). The filter's seed noise is about the size of the effect (problem 1). Blocked (methods_underspecified).

Cell 52: under O1 (a), 6 to 8 of 16 values match depending on O3 to O5, so the criterion's 8 is not reached under every reading. The DF-Q constant parameters differ (split a: alpha2 0.05, kappa2 -1.1, against 0.45 and 0.45). The sigma values are unreliable (problem 2). It asked for the training likelihood at the paper's values next to the optimum.

Cell 56: 9 of 9 means match under O1 (a) and 6 of 9 under O1 (b). The criterion requires every O1 reading (problem 9: tables 1 and 2 treat O1 as the parameterization, table 3 requires every O1 reading, and under O1 (b) kappa is on a different scale by construction). Blocked (methods_underspecified).
Cell 68: O14 (a) gives 80 and 33, an exact match. O14 (b) gives VP 37 against 33 +- 3.3. Blocked (methods_underspecified).

Cell 99: reward information is above threshold before the L/R entry in 16 to 28 of 23 to 28 windows, in every reading. Problem 5: the paper says only that reward information started to increase at the tone and lasted into the next trial, so pre-entry information above threshold is expected (about 5% of the peak) and the paper's qualitative statement is supported; this is a claims-file reading. Before entry also uses the median reaction time, not each trial's entry time.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the first revision (155 cells), the helper module, the claims file and the attempt record, with the paper. The verifier agreed with all 46 outcomes and found that round-1 points 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 11 and section C are resolved and point 2 partly. It quoted sentences the outputs do not support, all corrected, and asked that the reading of the partial rule and the initial value Qi(1) = 0.5 be stated. Report in transcripts/001641/verifier-2-report.md.

paper_notes.statement: The paper reports 60,221 trials, but its parts (39,175 choice, 12,707 no-choice and 8329 error trials) sum to 60,211, the number of trials in the dataset; the parts match the dataset exactly.

The Results say the constant-parameter Q models predict worse than the first- or second-order Markov models, but the reported F-Q and DF-Q (constant) values (0.531) exceed the first-order Markov model (0.528); the dataset agrees with the numbers (0.5306 and 0.5295 against 0.5283).

Question for the paper's authors. The Q update (Methods, equation 3) is an image missing from the text. Is the chosen action's value updated as (1 - alpha1) Q + alpha1 kappa1 after reward and (1 - alpha1) Q - alpha1 kappa2 after no reward (assumed here, as under it the paper's Table 1 and Table 2 constant values lie near the fitted optimum and all Table 3 means match, though Table 2 itself is not reproduced), or with kappa1 and -kappa2 added without the factor alpha1? Table 1 to 3 and the model comparison depend on it.

Question for the paper's authors. How were the 70 sessions divided into training and test sets? Alternate sessions in the order of the files (sorted by rat and session) gives exactly 19,986 training choice trials, as reported, and was assumed; the test set then has 19,189 trials, not 19,186. The paired tests of Fig. 5 (fig5-fq-dfq-beat-all-models, fig5-fq-dfq-no-difference) change outcome with the split.

Question for the paper's authors. With Qi(1) = 0, the local matching law P(L) = QL / (QL + QR) is undefined at the first trial and predicts one side with probability 1 after the first reward. What initial value, or what rule, gave its normalized likelihood of 0.508? A non-zero initial value (0.1 to 1.0) was assumed and gives 0.504 to 0.508.

Question for the paper's authors. What do the Mann-Whitney tests of Fig. 2B and 2C rank, the 0/1 choices of all trials following each history (assumed; it gives p = 0.92 to 0.94 for the Fig. 2C test the paper reports as 0.94) or per-session probabilities? Under the latter, P(L|R0 L1) against P(L|L1 L1) gives p = 0.01 to 0.03, not p < 0.0001.

Question for the paper's authors. How were sigma_alpha and sigma_kappa searched, and was the random walk of alpha bounded? With 5000 particles (split a, O1 a) the training likelihood of each model varies by at most 0.0074 over sigma_alpha 0.0025 to 0.08 and sigma_kappa 0.025 to 0.15 (at most 0.0035 for sigma_alpha up to 0.04), apart from one grid point where the filter collapsed in one session (standard Q under O5 a at 0.02 and 0.10, 0.398); with alpha clipped (O5 b) the best F-Q sigma_alpha is 0.08, the top of the grid. The fitted sigmas (Table 2) depend on the search.

Question for the paper's authors. In the state-coding test (Fig. 8B), were error trials with a cue tone included? Excluding them (assumed) gives exactly 80 and 33 state-coding units; including them gives 83 and 37.

entries.name: ito-2009
entries.title: Decision-making models and decision variables in the rat ventral basal ganglia (Ito and Doya 2009)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Ito and Doya (2009) on dandiset 001641, which holds the behaviour of six rats in 70 sessions of a probabilistic free-choice task and 214 single units from the nucleus accumbens and ventral pallidum. It covers the trial counts and choice history (Fig. 2), the least-squares and maximum-likelihood fits of Markov and Q-learning models with constant and time-varying parameters (Fig. 3 to 5, Tables 1 to 3), and the coding of state, action, reward and action values by the neurons (Fig. 8 and 9).
